title: Increasing the pressure of a gas

notes.definition: Work is the transfer of energy by a force. Doing work on an enclosed gas, for example by pushing in the piston of a bicycle pump, increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause its temperature to increase.
explanation: Work is the transfer of energy by a force. When a force moves an object, energy is transferred, and the amount of energy transferred is equal to the work done (work done = force × distance moved along the line of action of the force). Work done is measured in joules (J).

When you push the piston of a bicycle pump, you exert a force on the piston and it moves, so you do work on the air enclosed in the pump. This transfers energy to the air. The energy increases the internal energy of the air, that is, the total kinetic and potential energy of its molecules. Because the molecules end up moving faster on average, their average kinetic energy increases and the temperature of the air rises. This is why the barrel of a bicycle pump gets warm when you pump up a tyre.

In terms of particles: the piston is moving inwards when air molecules hit it. A molecule that collides with a piston moving towards it rebounds with a greater speed than it arrived with, just as a tennis ball bounces back faster from a racket swung towards it. So each collision with the moving piston gives the molecules extra kinetic energy. Across billions of collisions, the average kinetic energy of the molecules, and so the temperature, increases.

Doing work on a gas and heating a gas are two different ways of increasing its internal energy. Heating transfers energy because of a temperature difference; doing work transfers energy by a force moving a piston. If the gas is compressed quickly, there is little time for energy to be transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rise is large. If it is compressed very slowly, the energy has time to be transferred away and the temperature hardly changes, which is why pV = constant experiments are done slowly.

Compressing the gas also reduces its volume and the higher temperature makes the molecules move faster, so the pressure increases for both reasons: the molecules hit each unit area of the walls more often, and each collision is harder. This higher pressure is what pushes air through the valve into the tyre.
keyFacts: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
Work done is measured in joules (J); work done = force × distance.
Doing work on an enclosed gas increases its internal energy.
Increasing the internal energy can cause the temperature of the gas to rise.
Molecules rebound faster from a piston that is moving towards them, gaining kinetic energy.
A bicycle pump gets warm because work is done on the air inside it.
Compressing quickly gives a bigger temperature rise; compressing slowly allows energy to be transferred to the surroundings.
Heating and doing work are two ways to increase the internal energy of a gas.

keyTerms.definition: The energy transferred when a force moves an object; work is the transfer of energy by a force.
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Reducing the volume of a gas by pushing on it, for example with a piston.
A fixed mass of gas trapped in a container, such as a pump or sealed syringe.
A moving disc or plunger that fits tightly inside a cylinder and is used to compress a gas.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the warm bicycle pump
workedExamples.question: Explain why the barrel of a bicycle pump becomes warm when a tyre is pumped up.
steps: The person exerts a force on the piston, which moves, so work is done on the air in the pump.
Work is a transfer of energy, so the internal energy of the air increases.
Molecules hitting the inward-moving piston rebound faster, so their average kinetic energy increases.
So the temperature of the air rises, and energy is transferred to the barrel, which gets warm.
workedExamples.answer: Work done on the air increases its internal energy and temperature, and the warm air heats the barrel.

workedExamples.title: Work done on a gas
workedExamples.question: A force of 200 N pushes the piston of a pump 0.25 m. Calculate the work done on the air. Assuming no energy is transferred to the surroundings, state the increase in the internal energy of the air.
steps: All the work is transferred to the air, so its internal energy increases by 50 J.
workedExamples.answer: 50 J of work; internal energy increases by 50 J

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the only way to raise the temperature of a gas is to heat it.
misconceptions.right: In fact doing work on a gas, by compressing it, also increases its internal energy and temperature.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the pump gets hot only because of friction between the piston and barrel.
misconceptions.right: In fact the main reason is the work done on the air, which increases its internal energy and temperature.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think compressing a gas makes the molecules move faster because they are squeezed together.
misconceptions.right: In fact molecules speed up because they rebound from a moving piston with more kinetic energy; being closer together does not by itself raise their speed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think compressing a gas always raises its temperature by the same amount.
misconceptions.right: In fact a slow compression lets energy transfer to the surroundings, so the temperature rise is small; a quick compression gives a large rise.

realWorld: Bicycle and football pumps get warm in use because of the work done compressing the air.
Diesel engines have no spark plugs: the air in the cylinder is compressed so quickly that its temperature rises enough to ignite the fuel when it is injected.
Air compressors used for tyres and power tools need cooling fins because compressing the air raises its temperature.
higherTier: This whole subtopic is Higher tier only: work is the transfer of energy by a force; doing work on an enclosed gas increases its internal energy and can raise its temperature; explaining this for a situation such as a bicycle pump.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only and is not in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: Use the chain: force moves piston → work done on gas → energy transferred → internal energy increases → molecules move faster → temperature rises.
Say 'work is the transfer of energy by a force' word for word if asked for a definition.
For particle explanations, say molecules rebound from the moving piston with a greater speed (more kinetic energy).
Do not blame friction: the mark scheme credits work done on the gas.
Link temperature to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
summary: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
Doing work on an enclosed gas increases its internal energy.
This can increase the temperature of the gas.
Molecules rebound faster from a piston moving towards them.
A bicycle pump gets warm because of the work done on the air.
Fast compression gives a larger temperature rise than slow compression.

questions.question:
Work is done on a gas.
Why does the temperature of the gas increase?
options: The molecules move faster on average
The molecules get bigger
More molecules are created
The molecules stop colliding
markScheme: 1 mark: The molecules move faster on average
questions.explanation: Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Work done on the gas increases this, so the molecules move faster.

questions.question: What is the unit of work done?
options: Newton
Watt
Pascal
Joule
markScheme: 1 mark: Joule
questions.explanation: Work done is an energy transfer, so it is measured in joules. Newtons measure force, watts power and pascals pressure.

questions.question:
A gas is compressed quickly using a piston. The temperature of the gas increases.
Which statement explains, in terms of particles, why the temperature increases?
options: Molecules rebound from the inward-moving piston with greater speed
Molecules are squashed and become hotter
Molecules collide with each other less often
Molecules lose potential energy and gain mass
markScheme: 1 mark: Molecules rebound from the inward-moving piston with greater speed
questions.explanation: A molecule hitting a piston moving towards it bounces back faster, gaining kinetic energy. This raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so the temperature rises.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of doing work on a gas to increase its temperature?
options: Warming a sealed flask of air in hot water
Letting air out of a tyre
Pushing the plunger of a sealed syringe in quickly
Putting a sealed bottle of air in a freezer
markScheme: 1 mark: Pushing the plunger of a sealed syringe in quickly
questions.explanation: Pushing the plunger exerts a force over a distance on the gas, which is doing work. Warming in hot water is heating, a different way of transferring energy.

questions.question:
Heating a gas and doing work on a gas have the same effect on one quantity.
Which quantity?
options: the mass of the gas
the number of molecules
the size of the molecules
the internal energy of the gas
markScheme: 1 mark: the internal energy of the gas
questions.explanation: Both transfer energy to the gas and increase its internal energy. Neither changes the number, mass or size of the molecules.

questions.question:
Two students compressed identical samples of air in syringes by the same amount.
Table 1 shows how long each student took and the temperature rise of the air.
Why did the air compressed by student A have a larger temperature rise?

headers: Time taken to push in plunger in s

options: Less work was done by student B
There was less time for energy to be transferred to the surroundings when student A compressed the air
Student B's compression removed molecules from the syringe
Student A's compression created new molecules
markScheme: 1 mark: There was less time for energy to be transferred to the surroundings when student A compressed the air
questions.explanation: Both students did the same work on identical samples. In the slow compression (student B) the energy from the work done had time to be transferred to the surroundings by heating, so the temperature stayed close to room temperature. Compression does not create or remove molecules.

The end of the barrel gets hot when the pump is used to pump up a tyre.
Explain why.

markScheme: 1 mark: a force moves the piston so work is done on the air in the pump
1 mark: this increases the internal energy of the air / molecules move faster, so the temperature of the air rises
1 mark: energy is transferred from the hot air to the barrel of the pump
questions.explanation: The key idea is work done on the gas, not friction.

questions.question: Give two ways in which the internal energy of a gas can be increased.
markScheme: 1 mark: heating the gas
1 mark: doing work on the gas (for example compressing it with a piston)
questions.explanation: Both transfer energy to the gas, increasing its internal energy.

questions.question:
A tyre has just been pumped up. The warm air in the pump returns to room temperature.
Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the air is at a higher temperature than its surroundings, so energy is transferred to the surroundings by heating
1 mark: so the internal energy of the air decreases until it reaches room temperature
questions.explanation: Energy flows from hotter to cooler objects until they are at the same temperature.

questions.question:
A student says:
'The temperature of a gas can only increase if the gas is heated.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: doing work on a gas (for example compressing it with a piston) also transfers energy to it
1 mark: this increases its internal energy, so its temperature can rise without heating (for example in a bicycle pump)
questions.explanation: Work and heating are both energy transfers that can increase internal energy.

questions.question:
A piston is pushed in quickly to compress a gas.
Explain, in terms of molecules, why the temperature of the gas increases.
acceptedAnswers: temperature related to average kinetic energy
markScheme: 1 mark: molecules collide with the piston, which is moving towards them
1 mark: they rebound with a greater speed / gain kinetic energy
1 mark: so the average kinetic energy of the molecules increases, and temperature is related to the average kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Each collision with the moving piston gives a molecule extra kinetic energy; this is how work done becomes internal energy.

questions.question:
In a diesel engine, air is compressed very quickly in a cylinder. Fuel is then injected into the cylinder.
There is no spark plug, but the fuel ignites.
Suggest why the fuel ignites.
acceptedAnswers: compressed quickly so little energy lost
markScheme: 1 mark: compressing the air quickly does work on it, increasing its internal energy and raising its temperature (little time for energy to be lost)
1 mark: the air becomes hot enough to ignite the fuel when it is injected
questions.explanation: This is a real application of doing work on a gas to raise its temperature.

questions.question:
A gas can be compressed with almost no increase in temperature if the piston is moved very slowly.
Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: internal energy stays nearly the same
markScheme: 1 mark: there is time for the energy from the work done to be transferred to the surroundings by heating
1 mark: so the internal energy (and temperature) of the gas stays almost constant
questions.explanation: This is why pressure and volume investigations are carried out slowly, so the temperature stays constant.

questions.question:
A cyclist uses a hand pump to pump up a tyre. After a few minutes the barrel of the pump feels warm.
Explain why this happens.
Use ideas about work, internal energy and the motion of the air molecules in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: the cyclist exerts a force on the handle and piston, which moves a distance; so work is done on the air in the pump; work is the transfer of energy by a force; energy is transferred to the air; the internal energy of the air increases; air molecules collide with the piston, which is moving towards them; they rebound with a greater speed; so their kinetic energy increases; the average kinetic energy of the molecules increases, so the temperature of the air rises; energy is transferred by heating from the hotter air to the barrel; the volume decreases and temperature rises, so pressure increases and air is pushed into the tyre.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically linked explanation from work done, through increased internal energy and faster molecules (with the collision with the moving piston), to the temperature rise and the warm barrel.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): an explanation that links work done on the air to an increase in internal energy or temperature, with some reference to molecules.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'energy is transferred to the air' or 'the air gets hotter'.
No relevant content: 0 marks.
questions.explanation: Build the chain step by step. Friction alone is not the explanation the specification expects.

questions.question:
A sealed, rigid container of gas is heated. A different sample of gas is compressed quickly using a piston.
Compare the two processes.
Your answer should include how energy is transferred in each case and the effect on the internal energy, temperature and pressure of the gas.
markScheme: Indicative content: heating: energy transferred because of a temperature difference; volume constant; compression: energy transferred by work, a force moving the piston; in both cases internal energy increases; in both cases average kinetic energy of molecules and temperature increase; in both cases pressure increases; heating at constant volume: pressure increases only because molecules move faster (more frequent and harder collisions); compression: pressure increases because the volume is smaller and because the temperature is higher.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear comparison identifying heating versus work as the energy transfer, and correct effects on internal energy, temperature and pressure in both cases.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct statements about one method, or a simple similarity.
No relevant content: 0 marks.
questions.explanation: Compare questions need both similarities and differences. The key difference is how the energy is transferred.

questions.question:
A student has a sealed syringe fitted with a fast-response temperature sensor connected to a data logger.
Describe how the student could use this apparatus to show that doing work on a gas increases its temperature.
markScheme: Indicative content: seal the syringe with air inside and the temperature sensor inside the air; record the starting temperature (room temperature); push the plunger in quickly, doing work on the air; record the temperature during and straight after the compression with the data logger; the temperature rises quickly; then it falls back towards room temperature as energy is transferred to the surroundings; repeat with a slow compression for comparison, which gives a much smaller rise; repeat to check results; a data logger is needed because the change is rapid.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with quick compression and temperature measurement, and the expected result (temperature rise) explained in terms of work done.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant steps, for example push the plunger and measure the temperature.
No relevant content: 0 marks.
questions.explanation: A data logger captures the brief temperature rise before energy is transferred to the surroundings.
